newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean workers strike after labour law passed.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean workers strike after labour law passed.

text.p: Militant South Korean unionists called an indefinite strike on Thursday after the ruling party rammed a controversial new labour law through parliament that gives employers the right to lay off workers.

The outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions ordered a walk-out by all its 500,000 members after the National Assembly adopted the legislation along with another controversial law strengthening the domestic intelligence agency.
"We have called an immediate and indefinite strike," said confederation official Yoon Young-mo.
"All members will stay away from their work sites and hold protest rallies across the country."
The confederation is South Korea's second largest union umbrella body and controls workers at key export companies.
A spokeswoman for the country's largest union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, said a decision on strike action would be taken at a meeting at 10.00 a.m. (0100 GMT).
At around dawn on Thursday the ruling New Korea Party adopted the labour law with no opposition deputies present.
The hotly debated bill challenges near-total job security in South Korea by giving employers the right to lay off workers and adopt flexible working hours.

Thursday's surpise action by the ruling party threatens industrial turmoil in a country with a long history of violent labour unrest. Employers have previously threatened to replace workers striking over the labour bill.
The other law gives wider powers to the National Security Planning Agency to investigate people suspected of sympathising with communist North Korea.

South Korea's version of the U.S. Central Intelligency Agency (CIA) had been stripped of many of its investigative powers by President Kim Young-sam under an election pledge to curb the agency that once hounded the political opposition during military-backed rule.
Opposition parties are insisting the ruling party acted unconstitutionally in railroading through the two laws and have refused to accept their validity.
They accuse President Kim of trying to rejuvenate the internal security apparatus to launch attacks on his political opponents ahead of presidential elections next December.

The ruling party insists the National Security Planning Agency must be given sharper teeth to combat a renewed threat of subversion from Pyongyang, highlighted by the intrusion of a North Korean submarine in September and violent leftist student demonstrations.
